utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the time necessary for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke with Mr. Reid in our office. He wasn't able to give me a precise figure this morning. He said he was going to try to get seven people to work on it, but even with seven people he said it may take some weeks. He would have a more precise estimate for me either later today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that, I would not understand. This is a transcription exercise, not a translation exercise. So I look forward to receiving more information, but that would be unacceptable length of time for the provision of just over 200 pages of actual transcription.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will advise him, Your Honour. I understand that part of our unit that we have available to work on this have been working on a 600-page, I think, transcription regarding General Perisic. But I will report back to you either later today or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am conscious of the resource difficulties, but once priorities are decided upon, it's difficult to see why that should be the length of time. However, I hope you can give us more information later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Turning now to the question that arose at the end of yesterday's proceedings relating to Mr. Visnjic's application for further cross-examination. This has been a very difficult matter to determine. At -- at the end of the day, it does seem that Mr. Visnjic may have failed to appreciate the implications of the documents on which he seeks to cross-examine further. And in light of the welter of material in this case, that's understandable. The difficulty is compounded by the fact that one of these documents originally appeared on the list intimating the documents likely to be the subject of cross-examination and was then removed before the cross-examination by -- before the decision by Mr. Visnjic not to cross-examine. So in the circumstances, Mr. Visnjic, we will allow further cross-examination, but we are going to monitor closely where this goes, because as I say, when you read these documents carefully, the point that you think you did not fully appreciate can be divined without having to look at questions asked by Mr. Ackerman. So your right to re-cross-examination will be restricted to matters which it is absolutely necessary for you to explore to ensure that General Ojdanic's case is presented to us. So, Mr. Lazarevic, there will be a brief further cross-examination now by Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to have a few questions for you. In order not to place this on e-court, you probably know the document dated the 25th of May that constitutes a letter of General Pavkovic to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff in relation to re-subordination, P1459 is the number.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see this document on the 25th of May, 1999 or sometime around that point in time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, not in that realtime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, General, under which circumstances did you see the document the first time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As accurate as I can be, I saw this document -- well, there's a constraint. I know that I showed my document in 2005 to the investigator when speaking to the OTP. I had the feeling -- I seem to remember that I saw that document then too and discussed the subject, but really I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, that was around the time when you were preparing for trial.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I first came to the Detention Unit and when I spoke to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I'd like to ask you something about another document. You probably recall that report of the control inspection of the Supreme Command Staff, 3D692 is its number. That is the report that the control inspection of the Supreme Command Staff prepared after the tour and after gaining insight in the realization of the implementation of the tasks of the Pristina Corps. It is dated the 29th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that document here in court a few times and also while preparing for my defence I had occasion to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, am I right if I say that in the proposed measures that are mentioned in this document, there are two types of measures contained: One group that pertain to the command of the 3rd Army and what they're supposed to do; and the second set of measures that are supposed to be taken at the level of the Supreme Command Staff? So this is a report of the control inspection to the Supreme Command Staff that is proposing at the same time to the 3rd Army to do some things and also to the Supreme Command Staff, for them to do something as well.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that is the way in which control inspection reports are written. I recall that that was the way it was. We see right now on the screen the proposed measures what the army command is supposed to do, under number 1 and 2, and then what should be done at Supreme Command Staff level.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. 3D694 is what I'd like to have called up on e-court now, please. General, this is an order of the Supreme Command Staff chief issued on the same day when the control inspection report was written. In it the report is accepted, and as we can see in the last two paragraphs, the proposed measures are being turned into an order to the 3rd Army Command; and, on the other hand, in the last paragraph, the Supreme Command Staff shall implement the proposed measures on its side as described. My question is: In realtime, were you aware of this document perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that at that time I did see this document; however, from the army command, as far as I can remember, I believe that this order did come from the army command. I cannot confirm that I saw this document at that time, at the command post of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, General, could you please look at 3D700. In the previous document, there was an order of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff whereby he turned the measures proposed by the control inspection into his own order. Now, General, what we have here is the answer of the command of the 3rd Army signed by the Chief of Staff, Major-General Stojimirovic. Now I wish to ask you whether you, General, in the command of the Pristina Corps received the plan -- or rather, the order on the elimination of weaknesses in accordance with this plan. That is attached to this document.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the documents I saw not this document but the order that relates to the corps command. What is referred to is the plan that was addressed to the Supreme Command Staff somewhere towards the end of the war. I think that the date is later than the date on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at page 2 of this document. General, I don't know how well you can see here, but I do have a hard copy that I can provide for you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My question is whether you saw this document, the plan of eliminating weaknesses and omissions, whether you received it from the 3rd Army Command.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the document -- I saw the document in the process involved. There is no reason for it not to have arrived. I cannot confirm when it arrived in the corps command, but this plan of eliminating weaknesses after the control inspection - that is to say, what was to be done by the army command, including the order, and then there is the attached document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. A moment ago you said that you saw not this document but the order that relates to the corps command. Mr. Visnjic has pressed on, shown you the second page, and asked, Did you actually see this document? Can you answer that yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I am saying that that's not that document. It is addressed to the Supreme Command Staff, not the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I thought you said, and -- but the answer you were now giving seemed to be a bit different, suggesting you had seen this. Now, if you haven't seen this particular document, as you've now confirmed, Mr. Visnjic can go on and ask you something else if he wishes. But it gets confusing when you go beyond answering the particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, General, when you look at document P1725, General, do we agree that these problems that are referred to in this letter dated the 4th of June - that is to say, a day later - after the 3rd Army had already responded to the order of the Supreme Command Staff dated the 29th of May, these problems that are being referred to here, are they identical or do they correspond to the problems that are mentioned in the control inspection report of the Supreme Command Staff and for which an order had already been issued in order to have them resolved, that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer that question. These two documents are available for comparison by the Trial Chamber, and you can make submissions about them. Move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic, does anything arise for you to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, anything for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I have a number of questions I would like to ask. I wonder if you could assist us further in understanding the concept of a military territorial detachment. Can I take it, first of all, that members of such a detachment would wear a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wear military uniform only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What exactly were they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military territorial detachments are organisational units within military departments, and there are two independent military territorial detachments that are directly linked to the command of the military district of Pristina. There is a total of 24 military territorial detachments. 22 are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got the numbers from earlier evidence. I want to know what they are. What -- what is their particular responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military department, as a military territorial command, covers the territory of two or more municipalities: In the territory of Kosovo and Metohija or somewhere else, but I'm talking about Kosovo and Metohija. Every military department has a few military territorial detachments that are intended for securing military facilities. Further on, for taking over barracks when units of the army leave the areas of peacetime locations for securing some facilities of special importance for the defence of the country. That is the essence, in three sentences, of the basic tasks of these military territorial detachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who generally were the people who were assigned to these -- these detachments?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are people who are from that area in terms of their place of residence, in terms of the place where they live. They are not extraterritorial replenishment from some area outside the municipality. They are within the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What would lead to a person being assigned to one of these detachments rather than to a unit of the VJ or rather than to a regular unit of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are priorities according to the mobilisation rules in terms of assigning military conscripts. Priority number one is the replenishment or manning of wartime units of the Army of Yugoslavia. Those are brigades or tactical groups. Then certain -- the certain meeting of needs of the police or the State Security Service; then military territorial units; and so on and so forth. There are some other priorities. Civil protection, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does -- does that mean that the fittest and youngest are assigned to the VJ and then the slightly less fit and young go to the police, and so on, or is there some other criterion by which personnel are assigned in order to different units?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the criteria. Another one is the military evidentiary specialty, what it is they had trained for while doing their military service. If a man served on a tank unit while doing his military service, he cannot be deployed to the military territorial detachment, because these detachments do not have tank units. For the most part, these are reconnaissance units, infantry units. For the most part, infantry and logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is the principal distinction between their functions and the functions of the civil defence and civil protection?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil protection is a special category that existed even before military territorial units, during the times of the so-called Territorial Defence. Civil protection primarily deals with taking care of the civilian population in peacetime, in extraordinary situations, and also during the war. Then another component came into being within this total civil protection. These are civil protection units. That is of a more recent date, a more recent date, in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is. The civil protection had a task -- the civil defence, rather, had the task of protecting important civilian facilities like hospitals, waterworks, certain factories, bakeries, and what is required in order to have the vital functions of a town function, the power supply and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is, I think, a translation difficulty there. Which of these two, civil defence or civil protection, existed first of all?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil protection came into being when the army came into being. Civil defence came into the play later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the civil defence units are the ones that are more recent.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The distinction you've made is between the civil defence protecting installations -- civilian installations and the civil protection protecting the civilian population in peacetime, now -- and in extraordinary situations during the war. What does that actually mean in practice?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice, that means extinguishing fires, evacuating population that is at risk or material resources as well in that area. That means warning of dangers; that is to say, alerting to the population to something like that happening. Decontamination of an area and facilities if there was some contamination due to an accident or intentionally during the war when prohibited weapons are used. That means providing shelter to the civilian population, providing sanitary conditions, accommodation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And during peacetime, what was their duty?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, practically there is no difference, but in a war the disasters are larger scale and the civilian population is more threatened. When there are earthquakes, floods, and other natural disasters, civil protection units are engaged in peacetime as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And one final question for the moment on a military territorial detachment. Did they -- or were they mobilised only in wartime?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. These are purely wartime units that are activated once mobilisation is declared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have heard some evidence in the case that they were used to combat KLA activity. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some were at the state border itself. For example, the Strpce territorial detachment belonged to this small town of Strpce that is on the border itself. They kept this particular facility in order to prevent any incursions from Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly the date when they were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was carried out successively. The corps command took over the military district. The military district was re-subordinated to the corps command between the 7th and 8th of April. I think that sometime after that period of time, most of the military territorial detachments were mobilised. At this point in time, I do not have any more accurate information than that. But in principle, in succession, successively, like all other units of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next thing I'd like to ask you about is the-- something about the military court system. There appear to have been military courts attached to military territorial districts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Military courts and military prosecutor's offices are set up in a war, attached to the corps command and attached to commands of military districts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there were military -- yes, there were military courts attached to your corps, for example, and also to the Pristina military district; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. What are their -- what's the difference between these courts?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my knowledge of that distinction is as follows: I'm trying to explain first the military court and the military prosecutor's office attached to the command of the military district of Pristina. That jurisdiction is to deal with criminal offences within the military district and criminal acts perpetrated by civilian persons outside of the army but against army members in the whole area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor's office and the military court attached to the command of the Pristina Corps deals with prosecuting and trying criminal acts for units of the Pristina Corps' organisational composition, that is, criminal acts perpetrated by its own members against the army or against civilians, against property, against any other party, but it has to involve members of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Going back to the -- the district, military district court. You say that's to deal with criminal acts perpetrated by civilians against army members. I follow that. But you also said the jurisdiction was to deal with criminal offences within the military district. Is that confined to offences against members of the military?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if members of the military district committed any criminal act against any other person, but it has to be within the military district. It relates only to the establishment composition of the military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if there were two Roma, say, husband and wife, and the husband murdered the wife and neither had a connection with the military and this happened during the NATO aggression, which court would deal with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither. It would be dealt with by a civilian court that has territorial jurisdiction over that area. If one of these Romas committed a criminal court -- committed a criminal act against the army or members of the army, then the military court attached to the command of the military district would deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did the ordinary civil court system function, continue to function during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Your Honour, all I know is that there were five municipal courts and -- sorry, five district courts and nineteen municipality -- municipal courts that functioned throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we've seen documents that relate to some of the activity in them. The next matter I want to raise with you is the arrangement whereby there was duplicate reporting. You reported from the Pristina Corps both to the 3rd Army command and to the either General Staff or to the Supreme Command Staff. When was that arrangement first put in place?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documents we looked at, in the heading of the combat reports of the corps, I saw, I believe, the 12th April. But when was it ordered, by whom? It could have been ordered by the 3rd Army commander to the corps. But who ordered it to him, I don't know. I believe the 12th April is the first date of a combat report that was addressed to both the 3rd Army Command and the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Forgive me for saying, this but you seem very vague about this. And -- and you're -- you're the very man, I would have thought, would know about an exceptional arrangement -- an exceptional reporting arrangement being introduced.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say this, I am not saying it's 100 per cent sure. A day or two ago we looked at such reports, and on the 11th of April there was no such thing. There were no two addresses. 12th of April was the first date with two addresses. But it doesn't mean that even before that date a combat report from the corps went up to the Supreme Command Staff without the address indicating the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But the question I really want to ask you is: Why was this exceptional arrangement introduced?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: It doesn't mean that even before that date a combat report didn't go up to the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember a specific order or a specific explanation being given for that, but to me it was understandable. It was not unusual -- it was not usual and I knew that even a border battalion, according to procedure, would inform the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, skipping two command instances -- or rather, not skipping them. They would report both to the army and the General Staff. Now, concerning this, I really don't know for sure. I believe that it was important for relevant data from the ground to reach the highest level. I really don't see any precedent in this kind of reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, we've heard general after general go through the witness box here and a case presented to try to suggest to us that there are strict administrative rules within the army and these are being followed and these are the documents that have resulted from following these rules. And here we have a situation which is not exclusive, as you've just pointed out, to the Pristina Corps but is nevertheless exceptional. It's not part of the ordinary scheme of things. It's the sort of thing I would certainly, speaking for myself, have expected you to know about, to have known the reason for. Now, how would it -- how could it be done without you knowing why it was being required of your reporters?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the command of the corps, it was a technical problem, a technical issue. It was going to send the same report to two addresses. Otherwise, nothing is different. But it is my understanding that the Supreme Command Staff wanted to know directly from the spot a complete report on seven or eight pages with as many details as possible and to be able to monitor the defence situation of the country. That is my deep conviction, that that's what they wanted to know. As for who formally ordered it, when, I really can't remember a written order issued to that effect. I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you the impression even that -- that it was associated with a particular subject on -- on which it may have been felt insufficient information was being conveyed to the Supreme Command Staff by the ordinary channel of communication?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to see here also some reports of the Pristina Corps bearing the stamp of the Supreme Command Staff even before the 12th of April, so that -- if you ask me, that really cannot be the reason. If the 12th of April is the cutoff date, then I would be more inclined to believe that it had to do with what happened between the 10th of -- 9th and the 10th of April, the danger of a ground invasion, and that was a concern for all who were involved in the defence of the country and it was necessary to follow closely what was going on on that front line. I really have no doubt that that could be the reason you are looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was this -- Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I believe the witness said that the ground aggression has started, not the danger of ground aggression. It started between the 9th and 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll come back to that in a moment. The -- the reports you're referring to prior to the war, did they not relate to the investigation of criminal conduct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean reports from before the war. I meant only reports from the beginning of the war, combat reports during wartime -- before the 12th of April, I had occasion to see some here in the courtroom. I saw one. I don't know if there are more. But I want to draw your attention to this, because at that time those reports were cc'd to the Supreme Command Staff, forwarded, for their information, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Those ones, then, were they concerned with the reporting of investigation into criminal conduct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a question that I cannot answer with sufficient certainty. I really don't know whether they were or they weren't. I only wish to say that other systems too had the obligation to report on investigation and prosecution, the prosecution offices and judicial organs. I really can't answer this, because the judicial organs and prosecutor's offices very diligently reported. They provided us with much more information on what they had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic has corrected the transcript so that part of your previous answer was to refer to the ground aggression starting between the 9th and 10th of April. What do you mean by "the ground aggression" at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean ground attacks by large strong forces from the area of Albania across the state border against the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with fire support from the Armed Forces of Albania and the air support of NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the -- the personnel who were trying to actually penetrate your territory were the insurgents that fall under the name of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite precise, the bulk of the forces involved in the ground aggression were also insurgents and insurgent forces of the KLA, but those on foreign territory cannot be called "insurgents." But I want to draw your attention to something different. There were also armed units, even tank units of the Armed Forces of Albania that attacked the border, let alone the foreigners, the Atlantic Brigade from the US, et cetera. So combined ground forces and special units of NATO, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next subject I would like to ask you about is Crisis Staffs. Now, it -- that's a fairly common expression in the Balkans, but it perhaps means something different depending on where you are. What was a Crisis Staff in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally have very little knowledge about the operation of Crisis Staffs in municipalities and local areas in Kosovo and Metohija, unless I learned something from the reports of my subordinates. If you allow me, I can try to explain what it was based on the experience I had from the former Yugoslavia. I never have seen a Crisis Staff or a self-styled president of a local government. They set up those Crisis Staffs themselves in crisis situations, but I heard only of the Crisis Staff of Vucitrn and Podujevo. I don't know much about them. I don't know their structure. I can only speak about the general features of Crisis Staffs as a phenomenon that existed in our former territory. In Kosovo and Metohija this was not a very prominent organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The two you've mentioned, when roughly were they established?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learned of the Crisis Staff in Vucitrn from -- primarily from Prosecution documents shown here, where it was written that the president of the executive council is somebody named Doknic [phoen] at the beginning of the war and he dealt with those issues, but nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't mean to suggest you should have a -- an encyclopaedic knowledge of the documents. It's your own personal knowledge, and clearly that's very limited, and I won't pursue the matter further. I'll probably demonstrate my ignorance of the e-court system now, at least the actual practical operation of it. I'd like you to have a look at P1468, which is the record of meetings of the Joint Command, and it's getting to the right page that may be a problem. The 23rd of August. In the English version, that's K0228412T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will -- we need the bottom of the page in English. There isn't a B/C/S hard copy of this, Mr. Hannis, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is in my office, Your Honour. I could run up and get it, if -- if you're going to cover more than one page or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I do intend to cover more than one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will do that, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you have before you the beginning of the record of the meeting on the 23rd of August?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the date. The first thing I see at the top is Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't look right at the top. It could be anywhere. In the English, it's at the very bottom of the page, but ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it on my side of the screen. I don't see the 23rd of August. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will see that it says that a -- the three civilians we've heard so much about, Minic, Matkovic, and Andjelkovic, were not at the meeting but there were three apparently additional people. Can you read the names of the three others who were present.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Present: General Stevanovic, Obrad and Colonel Lazarevic V.," Vladimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's not a third one there that is difficult to read; there are only two names?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two. Two names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this appears to be the first occasion that -- that you attended this group of -- of people, and you've described already going to certain meetings. Do you remember Obrad Stevanovic being at the first meeting you were present at?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must confess that I did not know my colleagues from the police very well. I didn't even know their ranks. I knew they were from the MUP. But I really cannot confirm whether he was present on that occasion when I attended for the first time. It is recorded here that he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have at a later stage. I met him some before that even. But not that much. I wasn't even able to -- I wasn't even able to identify them all if they were in civilian clothing. I cannot really confirm that he was present then. But if somebody recorded this meeting, they probably recorded it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you remember being present at a meeting where the kidnapping of journalists was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the incident, if that's the one involving the kidnapping of two journalists around Orahovac. But I don't know to what degree and whether it was discussed at the meeting. I know that the OSCE mission got involved in the matter later. I know of the incident, but I really cannot remember any information exchanged at one of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you remember General Djordjevic being present at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that on those few occasions he was there -- I cannot be 100 per cent certain. But if we look at documents, we can check. I would say that on some of those occasions I saw him. But if -- I can only confirm for sure that I was with the corps commander. But as for the others, who attended when, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you would now go to the 17th of September. In English, that's page 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last four digits for the B/C/S, Your Honour, on that are 8514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that at the top right or at the bottom left, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the ERNs are stamped in various places on various pages. But they are sequential, and that may help the general find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's more than three-quarters of the way through. Do you have it? Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I found it in the printed version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you remember on these occasions -- on at least some of these occasions meeting Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. I think I did see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Minic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And on any of these occasions did you see Mr. Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did on some of these occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the one on the 17th that you're looking at records you as speaking and talking about attacks on your border observation posts. Do you remember telling the group about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, for the most part, I discussed that at those meetings. I provided information from the state border, firsthand information, if I can put it that way. I see in the first sentence here, if that is what you're asking me, that that - and well, the second sentence too - primarily pertained to what was going on at the border. Now, whether it was all in that order and that way, I really cannot recall, but for the most part I spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Generally at -- at these meetings, was Mr. Lukic present? I mean General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, on some occasions I think that he was present during this brief period. While I was in attendance, I think I saw him on some occasion. I may make a mistake, but I think that I did see him on some occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you go over the page now to the start of the record for the 18th of September. You've already read a little at the beginning of this to us in your evidence. This one suggests that you were reporting about the return of refugees, passing on reports you had got and various things you were having to do in areas where people were returning. Do you recollect if -- if that's something you would -- you reported to them on or explained to them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot -- well, there are six or seven bullet points here. I cannot remember all of that. But as for this first bullet point, via the Streoci mountains where the terrorists took civilians to Albania as a human shield and now they were returning them, this was a problem that was pretty big. I am aware of that fact, and I assume that I could have told those people present there about that too. Because you see, it says in parentheses here, "terrorists." I remember that problem, via Montenegro to Albania, they went there. We knew the terrorists went there. They were returning and that was the situation in mid-September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you could go forward now a couple more pages to the 21st of September. It -- the date has been written as "1 September," I think, but it should be 21 September, if this is in sequential order. Now, you're -- you're recorded as being present at that meeting. Do you know who Mr. Radovic is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic is an official from the State Security Service, a person from the State Security Service of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in this particular minute, there's no reference to any army report being made but there is reference to discussion of the involvement of international figures or countries in the -- the problem. At any meeting you were at, was that sort of thing discussed? For example, there's reference to Yeltsin's efforts, which we've heard about, and also about positions taken officially by - or perhaps not officially - positions taken by Russia and the United States.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot be that accurate. I know that as for these people who attended meetings from among the state officials, we received information from them that was of a political and diplomatic nature too. As for what you are asking me about, Mr. President, Your Honour, about the Russian position, Yeltsin's position, I cannot say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Do these questions and answers raise any issues for any Defence counsel other than Mr. Bakrac, any that you wish to raise? Anything for you, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there was one, regarding the discussion about civil defence and civil protection, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to ask if -- you asked about the distinctions between their functions and their roles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to ask if there were any distinctions in terms of uniforms, insignia, and weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you that question, Mr. Lazarevic. Between civil defence and civil protection, was there any difference in the uniform worn, the insignia, and the weapons carried?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw uniforms of members of the civilian protection; however, I personally did not see the uniform of members of the civil defence. I did not see that. I did not see weapons of the civil protection and civil defence. I know what is envisaged by the law, and I saw a document from their administration stating that they should store their weapons at army depots. But during the war, I really did not see any of these persons from the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what were the civil protection uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil defence uniforms -- civil protection uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Civil protection, yeah.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say they were light blue in colour, with insignia on the sleeves that were yellow triangles. And around the triangle is a circle. It is that type of uniform. Then a cap of this blue colour. They also had some vests, fluorescent yellow. And that is what I saw. Because, you know, the firemen of the civil protection wear one type of weapons; those for reporting wear others; and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what weapon did they actually have?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see them carrying weapons. I know what the law says, but I really did not see -- because I saw them extinguishing fires and getting the wounded out. I saw that on one or two occasions near Luzani Bridge on the 1st of May, 1999. But I did not see them with long-barreled weapons. I'm talking about the civil protection. The law says that they should only be armed with side-arms. It is the Ministry of Defence that regulates that particular subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was one other regarding military territorial detachments I -- I wasn't clear on. I understood that they come from the municipalities, but I wasn't clear if there were circumstances under which those detachments could be assigned to a task outside their municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've -- I think that question may be asked, but we certainly have had evidence that they were re-subordinated, and I -- I think the answer to the question is "yes."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, these are not local guards and Territorial Defence. It's not that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I had, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just go back to the civil protection and civil defence question. Just a moment, Mr. Fila. We've seen a number of documents in which subordinates are enjoined, at least, to utilise the armed non-Siptar population, and you have told us that that is largely a -- a reference to largely civil protection and civil defence. Are you saying you've never actually seen the civil protection or civil defence used in anger?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that, Your Honour, Mr. President. I did not see a single member of the civil defence, but I did see members of the civilian protection and units of the army getting people who were hurt out after the bombing of Pristina. I saw that. Not to speak of any attacks. I did not even see these people, let alone see them engaged in attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But -- but you know what I'm referring to, a number of documents which suggest that they should be used along with military or police units to actually engage the terrorist forces. Now, you've never seen that happen?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me. Your Honour, Mr. President, with all due respect, as far as I remember, the documents say that these forces are engaged for securing roads and vital facilities, not for active action against terrorists. So this is a position that is based on what their general purpose is and what the combat rules are. And that's only at the level of the general matters; namely, what I got from the army commander. As you could see, I did not expand on that, because I didn't know what detachment, what local guard. I didn't receive anything on that score. Had it been necessary, there would have been re-subordination and then some gorge or some bridge or some tunnel is something that they could have secured. But that would have to be resolved through a procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I stand corrected by you on -- on what was envisaged in these documents. But I -- I gather - please say if this is wrong - I gather you're saying that you never actually saw any of them used for any of the tasks that were mentioned in the documents we've seen.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, except for the civil protection once or twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that was -- according to you, that was to deal with the aftermath of fire or something similar.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after a fire and after a bus accident on a bridge. Their intervention was late. And our military intervention was late too. There was no help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm more concerned with their use in a positive way to secure installations or -- or roads, as you mentioned. You -- have you ever seen them used in that way?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't. It is possible that the administration for defence engaged them. I'm not challenging that. But as far as army units within the Pristina Corps are concerned, I really, absolutely -- not a single unit could not have used these civil protection units, and they didn't use them. And I believe -- well, if you want me to put it that way, I believe that they did carry out part of their functions within the defence system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything else, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I -- General, I would have a question. I seek some clarification with respect to the military territorial detachments. Now, as you were informing us about their functions on questions which were raised from the Bench, I gathered as if these were units who performed watch-and-ward duties, like taking care of the barracks, taking care of the equipment, and looking after these in the absence of the soldiers having gone outside. Now, that's what I gathered. And we know that there is always a unit like this which has been picked up from the local territorial limits to perform the watch-and-ward duties. But then later on the road as you went further, I learned that there were -- there could be -- they could be used beyond the local limits from where they are recruited; and, secondly, that they could also be posted on the borders and be with the VJ or the combat units. So a question arose in my mind as to how these people were recruited. And the second question was that if initially their duty was for watch and ward, wasn't it an aberration to send them on the borders? Why was this happening? So I have two questions. One is how they are recruited. And secondly, is it an -- was it an aberration from the main task for which they were meant to have been sent on the borders. I mean, if you could clarify this, because it looks a bit chaotic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order to be as accurate as possible, I gave the example of the military territorial detachment of Strpce. Strpce is a small town very close to the border with Albania and Macedonia. There aren't any military facilities there. There are no barracks there. This detachment of 200 or 300 people has nothing to guard or watch there. They are supposed to close a pass through which terrorists were coming from Albania and thus threatening this small town of Strpce that had a mixed population. It is within the territory of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade and it was their task to defend that area and to prevent incursions by terrorists from Albania. That is on the first point. As for the second point, these are not guard units. Within a military district, there are reconnaissance sabotage detachments. This is a special unit that is trained for anti-sabotage activities: Also there is a military police company at the level of the military district, that is to say, to carry out military police work. Within their weaponry, they have 60-millimetre mortars. That is to say, that they also have a anti-aircraft battalion, and that is to say that they can defend themselves from air attacks. So these are combat units that can secure and defend military facilities but also in terms of some military topographical positions they can guard them -- guarding the flanks of some of the other army units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And what about their recruitment?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the military district, they have their own command. It's the military district that mobilises them. There is a plan from earlier on, a special plan of mobilisation or a war plan whereby they are engaged, unless there is re-subordination. If there is re-subordination, then the new command engages them in accordance with their needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I apologise interrupting. I meant their initial entry into the armed forces. I mean, is the recruitment distinct and separate from those of the VJ? That's the question I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No. There is a single mobilisation plan. This is a single plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you wanted to raise something.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Don't be afraid. I didn't want to ask anything. I just wanted to help you. It doesn't say "the 1st of September." It says "the 21st of September." In the Serbian language, it says "21st of September." However the document's is gone. It's missing, it's no longer there. I just wanted to tell you that it was a question of the translated document. In the original this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse me. Mr. Bakrac, over to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, it's my turn again, but we are not going to be engaged in the whole cycle yet again, so you shouldn't be afraid. Since we are going to take the break in five minutes, I thought that I should deal with this in the same order in which the cross-examination went, so in order not to interrupt, I'll start with the basic points, how you and I started the direct examination. There were some misunderstandings in relation to who appoints generals and at whose proposal. In this connection, His Honour Judge Bonomy put a few questions to you. I would like us to clarify that matter. And may I ask you: Who is it that proposes appointments of generals? And in the General Staff, is there a special list of generals or potential generals? And if so, who keeps these records?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the personnel department of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, it is prescribed that there should be a list of the general personnel, of future generals, so to speak, on the basis of assessments, estimates, proposals of subordinate commands. Every calendar year this list is adopted at General Staff level. It becomes longer or shorter. So it is then -- it -- that is the institution at army level that takes care of this matter, these future generals. I, as a member of the collegium of the Chief of Staff of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia can say --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure how this arises from anything I asked in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's apparently something I asked, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that I did say that you were the one who asked about that. I really don't see why my colleague Mr. Hannis recognised himself in this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honour, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- I don't remember really wanting all this detail, but please continue if you think it's important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just one more sentence. It is the General Staff, that is the institution that keeps these documents and that proposes to the President of the State -- or rather, in most cases this was done not only to the President but to the Supreme Defence Council, and that is absolutely the procedure that I was aware of throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That will do. Let us just keep things as short as possible and we'll move on faster. So, General, can we conclude that the President of the Republic only formally adopts his presidential decree but the proposal comes from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just as well. The -- let's get the ground rules clear at this stage. Leading questions of that nature, conclusions that you seek to draw from the overall evidence are not appropriate in re-examination. It's open to you to make whatever submission you wish in due course about the role of the President, but that sort of question is out of place now at re-examination. It's perfectly in order for you to ask questions about the system and how it operated in practice, but not a question of that nature, Mr. Bakrac. And we will break now and we will resume again at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, my colleague or my learned friend Mr. Hannis asked you about your commendation from your personnel file, when and from whom you received it, and you were not sure about the date. Could we look at 5D1326, please. It's a personnel file. Could you look at the last page, please, page 9, column 15, and could you tell us whether that's what you were referring to and whether it refreshes your memory as to when you were commended. It's the last page, page 9, column 15. Line 5. The last page, under the heading "15."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the commendation or prize I was referring to, the prize of an official pistol received from the chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. I believe at that time it was General Ojdanic, although I may be wrong. And the date is the 21st of April, 2000. That's what I was referring to, even though I didn't have the document before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's move on. My learned friend asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, the indictment claims that General Ojdanic was named Federal Minister of Defence on the 15th of February, 2000, so he would not be chief of the General Staff at that time if that is true. Does that help you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not sure whether it was in early 2000. Now that I see the date, it probably was not by General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, my learned friend asked you whether members of the Pristina Corps were frustrated if a soldier was killed by the KLA. I'd like to know: When you became the corps commander in 1999, were there any events that might have caused frustration in the army and it did not happen?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to point out through my reply to Their Honours that in a professional army, there are, of course, frustrations but they cannot be what the members of the army are guided by. I want to give you a specific example. On the 8th of January, 1999, when terrorist forces kidnapped eight soldiers in broad daylight in peacetime, there can be no greater frustration for the entire state and for the army. This, however, does not mean there will be retaliation or that the army should disobey the rules. I know very well that we showed extreme restraint and acted very correctly, and I think the international representatives confirmed that at the time. I'm giving this by way of a specific example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I wanted to show you a specific exhibit, but I'll do it this way: Do you know which international representatives, if you remember, and how did they assess this event?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have seen documents here from Mr. Vollebaek, the chairperson of the OSCE, where he commended the restraint shown by the army and the state in their response to this major problem where the OSCE was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's 2D181. I don't think there's any need to delve into it any further and waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, my learned colleague Mr. Ivetic put a large number of questions to you which seemed to suggest that there was actually re-subordination of the MUP and that the Army of Yugoslavia, or more precisely, the Pristina Corps participated in the planning of actions for the MUP also. Could we please look at 5D476. This is your document of the 9th of April, 1999. Can you please comment on paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, it says that the staff of the MUP of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija issued an order to all the secretariats of the interior to start planning actions to break up the remaining terrorist forces. And with a view to coordination I commanded that the commanders get in touch with the heads -- the chiefs of the secretariats to see to what extent cooperation could be established with the MUP in carrying out that task in view of the information we had, the Pristina SUP, the Pec SUP, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on to document 4D229, dated the 20th of April. It's an order issued by the 3rd Army Command from the forward command post. Please comment on item 1. How did you understand this order? Who was supposed to contact whom?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 299. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a well-known order on re-subordinating the organs of MUP units to the army. In item 1, the army commander orders that those units and the organs should be re-subordinated to the Pristina Corps and Nis Corps and that the commanders of those corps through their orders, in conformity with the organisations of the organs and units of the internal affairs in areas of responsibility should regulate the duties in the planning and conduct of combat operations at each level of command. That means to establish the possibility of re-subordination at each tactical level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, you've just explained that this referred to the lower tactical level. My learned friend Mr. Hannis asked whether you were looking for counterparts in the MUP, someone who would be your counterpart. My question is: Did the 3rd Army at the forward command post establish contacts with the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on a few occasions, yes, as far as I know. There were some documents to that effect. But very, very little, because quite simply the situation did not allow for the army commander or the corps command to communicate or establish firm contacts with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Ivetic further showed you their Defence document 6D704. This is an order Bajgora 2 of the 4th of May, and here it seems you ordered the coordinated action with the MUP forces. Let's look at P9189 [as interpreted]. These are minutes from a meeting with the leading employees of the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija dated the 4th -- [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1989, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's the document, General. Would you please look at the last page, the fourth page, which is the last, and comment where there are asterisks, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven -- so the seventh one and the last one.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the seventh asterisk says: "Obrad Stevanovic, Assistant Minister." As far as I can understand the document, that's what he is saying, command and control of the units of the territory of the secretariat shall be carried out by the chiefs, the chiefs of the SUPs. And then the last: "Conduct cooperation with the VJ through the commander of the -- or commanders on the ground and inform the staff of any problems." So the Secretariat of the Interior is in command and they are cooperating with the army in the carrying out of these tasks, not just one task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At what level was this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the brigade commanders, combat group commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move on to P1996, dated the 7th of May, 1999. As I mentioned, 6D704, Bajgora 2, where coordinated action with the MUP is mentioned, that's dated the 4th of May. And these are minutes from a meeting of the 7th of May in the MUP staff three days later. Could we look at page 9. That's the page before last. Can we look at that first, please. The page before the last, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It says here that the head of the staff promised the minister, Lieutenant-Colonel Stevanovic -- he gave him the floor, that is. And could you please read item 2.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Anti-terrorist actions in certain parts were slow and with many problems. After the completion of larger actions, such as Budakovo-Jezerce, there will be independent planned work of each Secretariat of the Interior on organising anti-terrorist actions in their areas. The plan must be approved by the staff and it shall be carried out with manoeuvre detachments."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, Your Honours, it's page 11. I see that in the meantime ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And please, item 4. Can you just comment briefly on item 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this something that Mr. Lazarevic has personal knowledge of or are you putting to him a document that comes from a -- a source that he was not involved in?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only wish to ask him whether this is consistent with what he knows and his experience on the ground, whether there was re-subordination, cooperation, and coordination. That is something that might be consistent with his knowledge of events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are you saying he hasn't answered these questions in a -- adequately already in cross-examination, somehow or other you need to rehabilitate him, he has been undermined by Mr. Hannis? Because that's what re-examination is about. Re-examination isn't another opportunity to expand upon your case. Now, are you saying here that there is something that needs to be clarified about his position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my understanding was that Mr. Ivetic in his cross-examination attempted to undermine the case from the examination-in-chief, which is that there was no re-subordination, that there was only coordinated action, that the army planned its own actions and the MUP planned its own part in the activities. And I am trying to strengthen Mr. Lazarevic's standpoint, which he expressed in -- during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I can't see how putting this document -- what is this document exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is the record from the meeting held in the MUP staff for K and M in Pristina on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But Mr. Lazarevic has resisted any suggestion by Mr. Ivetic that somehow or other there was -- well, in -- he's resisted everything, I think, that was put to him. I may be wrong in some minor detail. But for you now to be putting MUP documents to him for his comment, it seems to me pretty pointless. These are things that you can argue about in due course. You can ask us to draw conclusions from them in light of the evidence Mr. Lazarevic has already given. But complete what you're doing on this, but please -- please try to confine your re-examination to things that need to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try, Your Honour. But in that case, please may I draw your attention to 1193 -- 5D1193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer to your question is "no." That's not what re-examination is about, drawing our attention to documents. Submissions in due course will be about that or presenting your evidence in chief and cross-examination may be about that. More particularly, examination-in-chief, but not re-examination. This is not a chance for you just to have another opportunity to supplement your case by reference to documents that haven't been explored at an earlier stage in the proceedings. That would give rise to the need for us to revert to Mr. Hannis and anyone else affected by that. It's issues that arose in cross-examination that need to be clarified that you should be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, precisely according to your instructions, just let me have a look at this and we will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I will have only one further question about re-subordination, something that Mr. Hannis raised and you mentioned too but you could not recall it precisely. It's the 37th Motorised Brigade. You said you seem to remember you sent some operatives there. Could we look at Exhibit 5D1084. Let us look at point -- 2.1, paragraph 6. Is that what you meant when you said that on the 17th of May -- Mr. Hannis said he was not able to find some documents yesterday. On the 17th of May you sent a number of operatives. Could you comment, which operatives were these?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the combat reports from the 37th Motorised Brigade from which we see that on the 17th of May as well I am making efforts by sending the assistants for operations, Colonel Stevanovic and another colonel, Novak Paprica, so that they can try to deal with the issue of re-subordination on the spot, re-subordination by those MUP units who were in the area of that brigade. And until the end of the war, these efforts remained fruitless. This is just one of those reports. And let me avail myself of this opportunity to point out that this is the Novak Paprica whose name I could not recall earlier. He was part of those efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- if I may. I -- perhaps there's been a translation misunderstanding, but the questions I had asked General Lazarevic about sending anyone to the 37th Brigade was whether that was to follow up on the allegations that MUP was involved in committing crimes. It wasn't about subordination or lack of subordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understood that General Lazarevic answered precisely to that question that that's why he sent operatives to the 37th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We'll move on soon to another subject, but I want to know: You were shown by Mr. Ivetic a map depicting an operation where some army units were drawn and some PJP units. Could you explain to us, what is normally indicated on a map for the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instructions on drawing maps of the Army of Yugoslavia stipulates that units up to two levels below should be indicated, as well as neighbours, as well as other units that are not within the system of subordination in that area but are known to be there, enemy forces are indicated as well as hostile territory. That is why we put on the map the MUP units that are known to be there. That is in keeping with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on. There have been quite a few questions about Operation Slup and Voksa and the order, that is Exhibit P1428. I think it remained unclear, and I think it's a good idea to look at 5D1174. That's a combat report from the forward command post of the 3rd Army dated 14 August. I would like your clarification and comment. Could we please look at item 4, which starts with the words "I hereby decide," on page 4. Just a second. General, this combat report relates to what day? We see that it's dated 14th of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means that it was written on that day, covering the previous day and ending at 1400 or 1500 hours on the day when the report is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, it covers activities of the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it possible that this decision of the 3rd Army commander was then made the previous day, on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the gist is this: The army commander made a decision to carry out this operation and ordered the Pristina Corps to support the MUP. That decision came into force when this report was sent to the chief of General Staff, General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. There have been quite a few questions and a lot of discussion here on the issue of the log number 455. Mr. Hannis asked you at one point whether that number related only to anti-terrorist activities. Could we please look at 5D315. Let us look at the log number, and you will tell us what this document relates to.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of my orders of the 10th May 1999. The number is 455-226, wherein I am warning units that there will be a medical examination of individuals experiencing psychological and other problems, behavioural problems. That number, 455, is given by the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Have there been other subjects covered in documents under the same number, 455?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in cross-examination as well we have seen at least several other documents under this number. I cannot recall exactly what they dealt with, but this is one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In order to move on more speedily, let me cite documents 5D359 and 5D365 that belong in the same category. Have there been any orders, General, to conduct anti-terrorist operations under other numbers, not 455?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The operatives who worked at that moment on the drafting of such documents sometimes put other numbers. It creates some technical difficulties, but it's not against any specific rule. It's not a particular breach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does -- does that mean that they should all have 455 as the reference number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to explain that what really matters is which organ created the document. The content can also decide the number, but as we have seen in our documents, the same subject was sometimes under 455, sometimes under other numbers. It was desirable to register it as 455, but it was not compulsory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, my learned friend Mr. Hannis asked you how much more evidence he needs to introduce, referring to the Joint Command, so that you admit to its existence. My question is: How much evidence is there about the activities of the Pristina Corps which contain no reference at all to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that during proofing we have prepared at least 4500 documents to tender, and then we abandoned that idea, and I know that this term is not mentioned anywhere in those documents. I know that for a fact. But I was trying to explain something else. Even in those places where there is a reference to the Joint Command, it is not proof of its existence, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We have seen -- you are saying that it's not proof that it really existed. We have seen minutes from those meetings where General Pavkovic reports that a special helicopter unit had not been established and two combat groups had not been established. If that had been the Joint Command, as suggested here, would it have had the strength, the power to create a helicopter unit and two special combat groups?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the point. And I am trying to make it to the best of my ability. "Command" implies power. The command decides. And if it's a Joint Command, it doesn't have to ask anybody. It decides. The -- the army commander in that case would have just decided, not approved. He has nothing to seek approval for. He just decides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't understand the point you're trying to make, Mr. Bakrac.
