That's exactly the situation that -- that Mr. Hannis is suggesting, that it's out of the individual control of the army commander, that the orders come from higher, and that's why you can't get your helicopter, because somebody else has to decide on it. I don't see how this point assists you. But perhaps you want to explore it more to see if you can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you have explained your understanding of the meetings of that group. Were they able to issue any orders?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of the Pristina Corps, as long as I was Chief of Staff in 1998, and in 1999 I don't even know where these people were -- it's not possible at all. But to the specific question of the Presiding Judge, I want to say this: This is not just about the helicopter. It's about two combat groups. There was a proposal to form two combat groups for the border. It's in the jurisdiction of the army commander and he doesn't accept these proposals. Whoever met wherever and suggested whatever, he doesn't accept it. It was only 45 days later that we managed to persuade him, telling him, "Look, the border is empty. There's no one." And that's when he changed his mind. And he was perfectly right. At that time, he resolutely rejected that proposal, and that was discussed in Belgrade. Even President Milosevic mentioned it. I -- I saw it in one of the documents. But I know that at that time he just did not allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This Joint Command, could it have issued any orders to General Samardzic, as commander of the 3rd Army, or to the commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't have ordered themselves or anybody else. I've already answered that. This document that we are referring to - and there are dozens of those - has no --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... calls for speculation on his part, whether or not the Joint Command could have issued orders to General Samardzic. For one thing, he says it doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, Mr. Hannis examined and stated in the indictment and is charging Mr. Lazarevic with being a member of that command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now we are proving that that is absolutely not correct and that that command as such did not exist, but it is in the indictment that Mr. Hannis wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if your allegation is that Mr. Lazarevic is a member of the Joint Command, is the question not one that he would be able to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it needs to be phrased differently, because his -- his position is it did not exist. Then the question should be: General, if such a command did exist, could they order General Samardzic to do such-and-such? And if that's the question, it calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It really -- Mr. -- Mr. Bakrac, it's a -- it's not assisting us at all to -- to go through this. Mr. Lazarevic's position on this is absolutely clear, crystal clear. What is it you think isn't clear? Because I -- to me there's a couple of questions in there already that aren't clarifying but confusing the issue. Move on to something different from this. Or at least a different -- even if it's the Joint Command, a different area from this particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I wanted to move on to another topic -- or rather ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis asked you about weapons and whether the Army of Yugoslavia issued weapons and military equipment to the MUP. Could we please have a look at 3D744 first of all. And then could you give us your comments with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document when General Pantelic testified, assistant chief of General Staff for logistics before the war; in the war, to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. My position was, as far as weapons and military equipment are concerned, it is only the Federal Ministry of Defence that is in charge of arming and equipping someone, because the federal ministry is the owner of military property. And this shows that the Supreme Command Staff is addressing the Federal Ministry of Defence in order to meet the needs of the police by ensuring some equipment and weaponry, because the Minister of the Interior asked the Supreme Command Staff for that. Even the chief of General Staff cannot pass a decision. He received this request from the MUP and he is forwarding it to the Federal Minister of Defence, and that can be resolved only at that level. I also answered that this was far away from me. I really don't know what was given, who gave it, and whether it was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Tell us -- there was a question as to whether the war diary of the Pristina Corps would state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're leaving this document, let's be clear. The -- the terms of this are that the Supreme Command Staff give approval to make these weapons available; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, my understanding is that this document was sent to the Federal Ministry for Defence and that the Supreme Command Staff was in agreement with this, but the decision has to be passed by the Ministry of Defence, not the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. He does agree with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you read then the -- the paragraph that begins "Pursuant to the request," at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On the basis of a request of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, strictly confidential number," et cetera, "dated the 7th of May, 1999, at the meeting of the collegium of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, held on the 11th of May, and the meeting of the collegium of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme" -- or rather, it says here, "the logistics assistant to the chief of Supreme Command Staff held on the 12th of May, 1999, approval was given to make the following available to the MUP of Serbia ..." So the Ministry of Defence is informed about this and they are going to make a decision to indeed have these resources made available to the MUP in the two ways described here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for it to be as clear as possible, could we please look at the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Underneath the table, could you just give us your comment with regard to the first paragraph underneath the table.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that "The administration for supplies of the ministry must make sure that the decision of the Federal Minister for Defence is to make a decision and a contract is made with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia on making available these mentioned resources." It's a complicated procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I see the English equivalent of that, please. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, the question was whether the war diary of the Pristina Corps would say where it was that you were during the course of the war, whether the combat reports of the Pristina Corps had entries pertaining to your movement.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, very seldom. Perhaps never. For a simple reason: Because I am to report to the commander of the army where I am and I'm with him every day, actually, so it would really be inappropriate for that to be written in the report of the corps command. I don't recall. Perhaps in one or two, but I really doubt that it's in a single report. For that reason, because the IKM, the forward command post, was at the corps command post, so I am going to inform him about other things, not that I was carrying out a control inspection with him on a given day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have clarification, because the question seems to be asking both about the war diary and the combat reports, and I don't know if the answer is referring to both or one. I understand those to be two distinct things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, could you have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps it was my mistake. I was referring to the war diary of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The question is just: Were you also -- is that what you meant as well, the war diary of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to explain. I meant the war diary. The war diary is a miniature of combat reports. The war diary for one day has perhaps one page; whereas, the combat report has six pages for one day. So the war diary is something where only brief entries are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's be clear on this too: The war diary of the Pristina Corps has as many combat reports as there are units; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The war diary does not have combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It is supposed to sublimate?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sublimate on this one page the combat reports of all the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you were asked in relation to P1967, the supplement to the decision on Malo Kosovo. Could you please explain whether a supplement to one's own decision is a legitimate way of working.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a few more questions on that. I tried to explain that a supplement is written when there are no radical changes and when there is no need to create a new document. Certainly this is the way in which decisions are made, through supplements to decisions too. In this way, supplementing the previous decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can look at P1483, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And could we hear your brief comments on that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw this document here during the course of the trial. The Supreme Command Staff on the 12th of April is supplementing its directive of the 8th of April with regard to certain tasks, certain pages, so they are adding or subtracting things. The Supreme Command Staff, due to certain needs, is adopting a supplement to the directive on the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, yesterday Mr. Hannis -- or rather, I think it was the day before yesterday. In this way you see that we are coming close to the end. Mr. Hannis asked you about your tour on the 29th of April of the 37th Motorised Brigade -- or rather, the 125th Motorised Brigade, and you explained that en route you came across a unit, part of a unit, part of the 37th Motorised Brigade, and you were shown document 5D384. Could you please have a look at this document of the 29th of April. Tell me -- or rather, would you read this. Since this is your document, please read the first paragraph. You can start from the point -- actually, could you read the first paragraph for us and give us your comment who it was that got stuck with a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 29th of April, 1999, around 900 hours, I personally came across part of the 37th Motorised Brigade which was crossing a brook near the Lozice village in disarray (next to the destroyed bridge), while the commanding officer was stuck in the brook in a passenger vehicle, bringing himself and other units in danger of being targeted by the air force."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to say what this word "officer" means.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw there an officer. Since he did not have any rank insignia in front, metal insignia, I thought that this was a reserve officer, a captain, who was in charge of that unit that was moving towards Klina. In my opinion, he thus exposed the unit to danger. I wrote to the brigade commander what he was supposed to do and to report back to me by the next day, 1600 hours on the next day, as to what kind of measures he took.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you said that on the same day you wrote an order to that effect. And my colleague Mr. Hannis suggested to you that in that way you wanted to return or punish the commander of the 37th Brigade. We are going to get to that. Could we call up in e-court 5D385. While we are waiting for the document to appear, in relation to the previous document you wrote "while the officer was stuck." If it was the brigade commander, what would you have called him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have called him by his establishment position, even the name and surname, because I know Dikovic. I don't know this man. I don't even know what position he had. I would have sent a different content had I found the commander of the brigade there in person, and I directly would have called him to account. I would not ask him to write a report to me as to measures taken vis-a-vis a third person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please look at this document now, 3888-1 -- rather 888. It's strictly confidential number, rather, the document is 5D385. And comment briefly to expedite matters only on the first paragraph. And tell us, where did you notice irregularities and what units did you warn of irregularities?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, although I didn't see the document, I said that on the same day I wrote another order, a warning, for the 37th Motorised Brigade and the 354th, 7th, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the aspect of their behaviour in combat, their conduct, and I sent this to all units as a warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's now look at 5D1020, dated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, did this mention the incident with the 37th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a general part, Your Honour, where it says "uncontrolled movement." But that's gone from the screen now. I know that in the preamble, that's the part where it's mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the document before me. I can read out that part, if you wish. By your leave. By Their Honours' leave, could we have the document brought back on the screen, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is on the screen, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on our screens, Your Honour. That's the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm reading this one thinking it's the -- another page of the same document. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D385.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the previous one was 5D384 -- oh, no, sorry. Sorry. You're correct. 5D385.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 3, after the comma: "There are daily occurrences of uncontrolled movement of the men in the area of defence and outside it." That's what I was referring to when I saw that unit in disarray crossing the brook and the aeroplanes flying overhead. This refers to the 37th. But I was trying also to draw attention to similar omissions on the part of other units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is it this, Mr. Hannis, that you're suggesting was done to humiliate the commander of the 37th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because you'll recall on the 20th of November, when I asked about this, page 18659, at line 18, I asked specifically: "Is that Dikovic you're talking about when referring to the commanding officer in the passenger vehicle?" And the answer was: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And that's being -- I think was to be followed up. But the discussion then was about whether something had been issued to all the commands which humiliated the commander of the 37th Brigade. And presumably this is the only document that could fit that category. And it doesn't seem to -- to mention the incident specifically at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought -- it was my understanding from my questioning about that document, 5D384, that that had been circulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It -- that it had been. But its terms don't look like it would be circulated; however, no doubt we can hear what you all have to say about that eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as Your Honour said, this needs further clarification, could we look at another document. I've got an echo in my headset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not saying it needs further clarification, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want to show one more document and then we can round off this topic concerning the 37th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please look at 5D1020, dated the 1st of May, 1999, and comment briefly on this document and tell us whether from the tone and the way it's written one can conclude that Dikovic was the one who was in the vehicle that was stuck.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the middle of this text, the commander of the 37th Brigade is writing to his subordinates that the corps commander personally - that refers to me - and the military police organ found a large number of the members of the brigade outside the area, outside where they had permission to go, and a group was found in the village of Lozica near the destroyed bridge. So he is telling his subordinates that I, as the commander, personally found not him but part of his unit. And he refers to my order, as you see, and then he issued a specific order as to what the unit should do, and that's on the second page in the continuation of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please just read where it says in the vicinity of Srbica there was an ambush and an attack on a motor vehicle -- on some motor vehicle in which was the assistant commander for the rear of the 37th Motorised Brigade, who was traveling without a security escort and special vehicle. Two men of the brigade were killed, and so on. Thank you, General. I have only a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you proceed, I identified one other thing that I'd like to ask about. Could we have P2809. This is one of the documents I was thinking about when I was asking you about the role of the armed non-Siptar population. Look, please, at paragraph number 3 of the order and just read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Into the system of defence and control of the territory in the area of responsibility, in addition to the establishment units, attached units and MUP forces, through the military departments, include the new military territorial detachments and the armed population in the zone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that appears on the face of it to be suggesting the involvement of the armed population in the general defence and control of the territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a somewhat altered sense, but essentially, yes, that's what it says also in the order for defence, because this refers to the system for the defence of the country. I'm trying to say the following: If there was occasion to use a structure outside the army for specific tasks, the procedure of re-subordination, subordination, command, and so on, would ensue. But this comes from the order for defence. It refers to the defence of the country. That's what was given at the level at which it was given, and quite simply that's how it was transmitted. But whether it would happen, well, if -- if it was to happen, there would have to be further specific orders and re-subordination mentioning time, place, role, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Attached to that document there was a plan of engagement of the joint units with their activities and tasks. Can you remind me what that set out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollection, Your Honour, there was a map of the deployment of the corps units and particular police forces with locations which were known, and there was a text on two pages accompanying the map which said what brigade was responsible for combat control of its own area and where there is a possible coordinated action with the MUP forces. I am convinced that nowhere did any other structure appear either in the map or in the text attached to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, yesterday my learned friend Mr. Hannis showed you PD372 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 5D372. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And asked you about it. That is, about removing civilians from the area of activities, military activities. And then there followed a question as to what the zone of responsibility of the brigade was. Could you explain the difference between the area of responsibility and the area of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of responsibility is a large piece of territory on which a certain army unit can be used for a certain task; whereas, an area of combat activities is an narrower category on a certain axis in a certain part of the former area where a military activity is going on; it's underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a specific reference to where I asked the question? Because I believe I was asking the question from the document, and here the document talks about "zones of defence," which may or may not be something different from "zone of responsibility" and "area of combat activities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a page reference, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the moment I don't have a page reference, because I agreed to changing our method of work yesterday afternoon, and this morning we are in -- well, I know it's P -- or rather, 5D372, which was opened by my learned friend and questions to this effect were put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the reference to "zone of defence," Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just looking at the document, which in item number 3 says: "Speed up returns of civilians. Do not allow civilian refugee groups to remain in the zones of defence of Brigades."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll see that in the immediately preceding paragraph it's "zone of responsibility." So that seems to be a basis for the question. So please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have a reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, when my learned friend yesterday commented on document-- the document containing the order to abandon schools and other buildings, he asked you whether these were the civilian targets targeted by NATO, and your answer was "yes." My question is: Were these the only civilian facilities targeted by NATO or were there others of a different kind?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to enumerate them all, all the civilian targets targeted in the air-strikes. It's not just schools. Mostly it was industrial compounds, parts of settlements, the road infrastructure, trains, buses, the transportation infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, just one final question. Could we please look at Exhibit 5D475. Yesterday my learned friend Mr. Hannis questioned you in detail about a number of documents dating from 2001, and I would only like you to tell us from your document the requests addressed to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, what were you referring to when at the end of the second paragraph and -- where you say that "a precedent has been set in the functioning of" -- what did you mean by "precedent"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I meant was as an officer this is the first time in my experience that somebody at that level is degrading, derogating, and undermining the Law on Defence, Article 3, which says that the commanding officer is in command of the units. It cannot be a coordinating body. So for the first time, as a lieutenant-general or even colonel-general, I saw something like this, and I did not want to participate in this kind of violation of the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. That completes your evidence. What we'll do is have the break now and resume at quarter to 1.00. By that time you'll be back in your place and the seat will be vacated for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is General Krsman Jelic. But before he is brought into the courtroom, may I ask for your leave to raise two questions? The second issue is technical. My colleague Mr. Bakrac did raise the issue of Racak on the 15th of January during his cross-examination of -- during the cross-examination of General Lazarevic, and that was on page 18547. And Judge Bonomy gave a clarification. It was during cross-examination by Mr. Hannis. The witness who is coming can give us the most relevant information about this incident, because the units of his brigade were deployed in that location. However, in the belief that Racak would not be discussed, we did not include in our 65 ter notification this issue. However, seeing the developments, we introduced into e-court two documents related to that location and that period, of which we notified our colleagues from the Prosecution and provided them with copies of these documents. I now ask your leave to question the coming witness on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, have you anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Kravetz is going to deal with this issue, I think she's prepared to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As Mr. Cepic just said, we have not been given notice that this issue would be dealt with during the testimony of this witness. And I have just been provided this morning with two exhibits that he wants to introduce through this witness. We haven't really -- prepared to deal with this matter. But if Your Honour is going to grant the Defence leave to deal with the issue of Racak, then I will be dealing with it as well in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're saying but for the fact that it's raised by Mr. Cepic, you would not have been raising it with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, I would have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I will allow you do that, Mr. Cepic, but obviously within the bounds we've already set in relation to that subject and we'll allow you to use the two documents you've referred to. And what's your second point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I discussed that issue, that technical issue with Mr. Haider during the break. If you'll allow me just one more thing. Listening carefully to what my learned friend Ms. Kravetz said, I understood that the issue of Racak is not so relevant for the Prosecution, because they did not prepare for it and did not plan to discuss it. But if they maintain this position, if this issue is not relevant in the view of the Prosecution, then maybe we need not waste time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's for you to decide as things stand, I'm afraid, Mr. Cepic, because there has been some evidence relating to Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is General Krsman Jelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jelic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you please -- can you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: General -- Major-General -- retired Major-General Krsman Jelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: 7th of April, 1947 in Podujevo. That's Kosovo and Metohija, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us about your schooling.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I finished primary and secondary school in Podujevo, military academy in Belgrade. I completed all possible training in the Army of Yugoslavia, finishing with the School for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the most important positions you held in your career?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I was mainly in command positions: Company commander, battalion commander, detachment commander, light brigade commander, mechanised brigade commander, armoured brigade commander, chief of Pristina Corps, chief of the operative group for dealing with the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija, in -- in the south of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please slow down a little. The interpreters cannot keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Nis, Leskovac, Vranje, Urosevac and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, speed of questions may be a problem, so could you try to concentrate on slowing down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do that. I will follow your instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please slow down in your answers so that all the questions and answers could be recorded properly. Now, would you please tell me, when did you occupy the position of commander of 243rd Mechanised Brigade of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of that brigade from May 1994 until 31st December 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, could you please tell me, what were the focal points of activity of that brigade that you led until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: The focus of our activity was on combat training, securing the state border, securing military installations, securing the main roads, and several actions of support to MUP forces in anti-terrorist actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that main roads were in danger and you secured them. Could you tell me, which main roads were the most hazardous?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: The greatest risk was to the road Pristina-Stimlje through Crnoljevo, Dulje pass towards Prizren, and roads towards Macedonia, through Kacanik to Djeneral Jankovic border crossing and from Globocica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 5D685, please. 568, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General -- while we're waiting for the document, what was the engagement of your brigade in in-depth securing of the border in early 1999?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Since there was a continuous onslaught of terrorist forces and smuggling of weapons and equipment from Albania and from Macedonia, the federal government took the decision that some of the units should be engaged in in-depth security of the border. Their main task was to support the 57th Border Battalion, that was line security and in-depth security to stop terrorist forces from spilling over from Macedonia and Albania and from crossing back into those countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we scroll down the document. Unfortunately, it is not the correct document. I requested 5D685, please. That is -- that is the correct document. We also have translation. Could you -- could you scroll down. I need count 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please look at the bottom of the screen. Let me first ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the heading. Is it your document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document from my brigade, strictly confidential number 108-2, 11th January, 1999, securing the state border, order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the document a little bit scrolled down. [Interpretation] General, look at item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in English, please, also count 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was that the priority, to secure the state border, as we see in this order? Was that the priority of your activities?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the priority task of the brigade the secure the state border, as written here. Continue to carry this out as the priority task of the brigade as in peacetime. Deadline: Continuous task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, this order, you issued it on what basis?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: It was issued based on the order of the commander of the Pristina Corps. I think that is indicated in the preamble.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, where and how did you conduct combat training of troops before the war until the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: We conducted combat training according to the training plan, mainly in barracks, on training grounds, shooting ranges, the usual locations we used over the previous 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In this courtroom, we heard some witnesses of the Prosecution who stated that the units of the Pristina Corps carried out large-scale exercises and manoeuvres in the areas of Albanian villages of Lasic and Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: From 1994, since I became commander of that brigade, until the end of that war, not a single large-scale drill was held on the level of the Pristina Corps. Never on a larger scale than company level or platoon level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was there any exercise that could intimidate the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No such exercises existed in the plan, and we certainly did not conduct them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system document number 5D686, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from my brigade. Strictly confidential number 186-2, dated 15 January 1999, maintaining and upgrading combat readiness, order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On what basis did you issue this order?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: As we see in the heading, it was issued pursuant to the order from the Pristina Corps Command, 105-1 of 15 January 1999, with a view to ensuring the required level of combat readiness in the forthcoming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please answer more slowly to the questions I ask.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you in advance. Would you please look at item 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the document a little bit scrolled down. This is the first page in B/C/S. Thank you. And in English, probably on the second -- actually, the first one, bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we don't need to read this paragraph of your order, but tell me, to what maximum level was training performed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: As I stated a moment ago - and we can read in this order - we conducted training up to company level. That was the highest level of training in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask you a few questions on a different subject; namely, the terrorist attacks. When did they intensify in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija; namely, municipalities of Urosevac and Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Terrorist attacks intensified in the spring of 1998; particularly, in April, May, and June. Those terrorist attacks were extremely strong and powerful on main roads where civilians were intercepted, robbed. There were lootings of equipment. That was the main point of terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system Exhibit number 5D057, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, tell us just very briefly, what is this document and what is it about?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: This is an official note dealing with an attack by terrorist forces that attacked a logistical column providing supplies to Dulje. They were attacked, wounding six soldiers, one of whom succumbed to his wounds in the Crnoljevo Gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you read when this happened?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of June, 1999 [as interpreted], in the area of Crnoljevo village, that is, in the Crnoljevo Gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was that year?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Apart from this, were there more dramatic attacks on civilians?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: The terrorist forces, as I said, were building up. There were an increasing number of ambushes and attacks. Perhaps the most dramatic occurrence in Kosovo and Metohija happened between Mount Crnoljevo and Drenica in the area of Klecka, where we detected a dozen victims approximately who had been cremated in the same year, approximately in the same period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Which terrorist brigades were there in the area of Kacanik and Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: In that broader area, there -- that was the so-called operative zone of Nerodimlje. There were units from the 161, 162, and 163 Brigades. The first two brigades were completely mobilised and activated and conducted combat operations; whereas, the third brigade was set up later, in 1999. Their strength was approximately between 1500 and 1200 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In addition to the brigades, within the terrorist forces was there a special territorial component as well?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. One can say that this brigade has a manoeuvre component and the territorial component was present in smaller villages and hamlets. We believed that there were about 40 such villages and hamlets. And in every one of them, there were between 100 and 150 members of these units, respectively, which is a total of 4 to 6.000 members altogether, and perhaps there is a margin of error of 15 to 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a bit of clarification. This territorial component, is it included in the brigades?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, it is outside the brigades. These are practically local guards in certain settlements that at a given signal mobilise people who serve as the alleged defence of the core of that village or kernel. And the brigades are of a manoeuvring nature and they moved in different places in Kosovo and perhaps even all the way down to Metohija as well. These are manoeuvring forces, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, was there a spillover of forces across the state border?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a spillover of forces, especially towards the Republic of Macedonia and from the Republic of Macedonia and to the Republic of Macedonia. Along with this spillover, there was large-scale smuggling of military equipment and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the Republic of Macedonia, were there any terrorist forces?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: According to the intelligence that we had, our intelligence, there was an equivalent of four brigades. At the time, we called them the 3rd, 4th, 6th, and 8th. And they were along the border with the Republic of Serbia, and their equivalent was roughly the brigades that were on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija; that is to say, between 1500 and 2.000 fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you explain -- could you explain whether this figure that you gave, 1500 to 2.000 fighters, is that the total number in relation to all brigades, or is it a question of individual brigades? Is it the strength of individual brigades?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: When I said that the figure was between 1500 and 2.000 brigades [as interpreted], it meant one brigade only, so then time it is number of brigades. That could be taken as the equivalent of the other side that was under weapons, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We mentioned the term of "spillover" of forces. Could you explain briefly what that means.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That means that forces went to Macedonia and came in from Macedonia. The term itself, "spillover," means moving from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I shall deal very briefly with the stay of the OSCE mission in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Could you tell me what kind of cooperation you had with the mission of the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: The corps commander issued -- the corps commander issued an order, and therefore in brigades, including my own, we set up a team that was duty-bound to liaise with the OSCE. There was an officer who was the head of this team, and through the mission that was in Pristina - that is to say, with the team that was from the Pristina Corps as defined by the order of the commander of the Pristina Corps - this cooperation took place; that is to say, from me to the liaison officer to the mission that was in Pristina and with the OSCE mission at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, how was the question of touring units in the border area resolved by the representatives of the OSCE, members of the OSCE mission?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Mission -- members of the OSCE mission were duty-bound to announce their tours in the border area, because already in that period there was reinforced in-depth security of these units and part of the area was mined as well. So for the sake of their personal safety, it was requested that they always announce their visits and provision was made for them when they announced their visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: They had to announce their visits how far in advance?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Roughly 24 hours, unless there would be a very exceptional incident when they had to react straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, General Maisonneuve testified before this Honourable Trial Chamber and he was head of the OSCE mission at this time, and he referred to a situation on the 8th of January, 1999 when there was an incident on the road between Urosevac and Stimlje. On that occasion, three members of the MUP were killed, and a few minutes later from a position at Dulje a tank appeared and fired a shell in the direction of the village of Slapuzane. That was also recorded in the proceedings against Slobodan Milosevic, and the transcript page is 5784. Maisonneuve claims -- General Maisonneuve claims that the army used a tank against the terrorists, which would constitute excessive use of military force. Please, do you remember a specific incident when three members of the MUP were killed? And the second part of the question is: Was a tank used on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: As for this information, regarding the killing of three members of the MUP, I know about that. I cannot recall the exact date right now. As for the opening of fire, I remember that allegedly fire was opened by our forces at Dulje. I state here that there was no need, no reason to open fire at the village of Slapuzane. Further on, this village is about 6 or 7 kilometres away. There was a ban on the use of ammunition, especially ammunition for large calibres. We sent daily reports on ammunition spent. Not one of those indicators confirmed this statement of Mr. Maisonneuve and it is certain that there was no shooting. On the assumption that it was necessary to fire, there were some three or four villages or hamlets that were much closer from which these hamlets can be seen and Slapuzane cannot even be seen from up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you just tell me: You're a tank man yourself, according to VES. Is it technically possible from this position at Dulje to fire at Slapuzane, to target Slapuzane?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: As for the positions at the Dulje pass, in the camp, it is technically impossible to fire from there for the following reason: Below is the village of -- sorry. There is a plateau, Boja, from which you cannot see the village of Slapuzane, so you cannot target it. A tank fires in a straight line, not a curved line; therefore, it is impossible to target in this way. This entire area in front is Birac and including the summit, Boja.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that this situation was checked by the higher command as well within the Army of Yugoslavia, as to whether this had actually happened?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Whenever there was an excess, they always checked things for us, the brigade and the higher command, and this was the corps command and sometimes even the army command. I know that a team came and checked everything, and all of this was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system 5D646, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you tell us whose document this is?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the command of the 3rd Army, the team for liaison with missions. Strictly confidential number 8098-11/77, dated the 14th of January, 1999. It's a telegram, very urgent, regular weekly report, the one that was submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... page number 4; in English, it's page -- also fourth page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, would you please take a look at the second paragraph, the third bullet point. It says: "From 1330 hours to 1340 hours" --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: "At the time from 1330 to 1340 hours the liaison officer from the Urosevac Garrison met with the representative of the regional centre of Prizren, Mihajlo Krasnoverski, who reported that on the 8th of January, around 1300 hours, after the attack of the Siptar sabotage terrorist forces, a tank from Birac fired at the MUP from the village of Slapuzane. When we checked with our forces at Birac and Dulje, this report was refuted."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this document confirm your words, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Precisely this is the document that was sent from the army command, confirms what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, was there an escalation of terrorism in February and March 1999 in the territory of the municipalities of Kacanik and Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Terrorism grew during February and March 1999, especially in the areas of Kacanik, Urosevac, and primarily on the roads that I referred to, from Kacanik, Djeneral Jankovic, from Doganovici to Globocica, and across the Crnoljevo gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there cases of urban terrorism?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: As these forces grew, these brigades -- I told you that there had been two, but by now already a third brigade had been established -- the territorial component was reinforced and terrorism slowly started moving from rural areas to urban areas. There were a few attempts, terrorist attacks in several localities in Kosovo and Metohija, primarily in Pristina, Podujevo, and in Urosevac there were three or four such explosions in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the withdrawal of the OSCE mission, how did the situation develop?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: As the OSCE mission withdrew from Kosovo, the terrorist forces -- well, for them it was practically a signal to attack all positions of the units that were in the area and in the border belt. Particularly fierce attacks came from Macedonia and from the interior -- or rather, from Kosovo and Metohija towards units that were engaged in in-depth security and line security. There were a few casualties among the soldiers then, and especially there was fighting for two repeaters, at 881, feature 881, that is, to the west of Djeneral Jankovic, and at the transmitter of Bojevo going to Globocica on the slopes of Sar Planina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What happened with the repeaters previously?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: These repeaters -- an attempt was made to take over these repeaters and destroy them, so there was fierce fighting there. If I'm not mistaken, the corps commander sent a helicopter then to get the lieutenant and the two soldiers out, those who were casualties at feature 881; that is to say, to the west of Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, at that moment and during the preceding weeks, was the NATO intervention becoming more and more of a possible reality?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: According to the information and the reconnaissance that we had, the aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was practically certain. First, one brigade came to the Republic of Macedonia, and then there was a buildup of forces and they had already reached the level of four or five brigades of the multinational forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, when did your forces leave the barracks?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: All the brigade units left the barracks by the 24th of March, 1999, just before the air-strikes began, and they took up positions in certain areas, and these were defence positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, these defence positions, were they in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Defence positions are chosen tactically, not in built-up areas. And for my brigade and probably all the other units as well, they were outside built-up areas. They were chosen according to tactical position, not according to built-up area. Those areas were chosen which would provide for the most successful and best defence from aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 5D1337, please. And could I ask the usher to pass this map in hard copy to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what does this map represent?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: This is the defence operation of the Pristina Corps. This is an excerpt for the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. It's an excerpt from the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please indicate and explain the area of zone of defence taken up by your brigade.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Before -- in front, there was the state border in a length of 808 -- 880 kilometre -- 88 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the border was 88 kilometres long in that area from the Danube to the peak of Sar Planina, the mountain, Sar Planina. Near the Danube was the village of Mirosavlje [phoen], that was to the right. And to the left, over the mountain of Sar Planina, Nerodimska Planina, up to the Dulje Lake. The total front line was about 150 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It might be more useful if you were to indicate this on the ELMO. That's the apparatus on your left. Or maybe on the electronic map. Whatever you find easier.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I'll try. This is the border towards the Republic of Macedonia. Then to the west, over Sar Planina, the Jezersko Mountains towards Dulje. And to the East, from the Danube, which you can't see very well here, towards Mirosavlje. So that's the border, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we -- excuse me, Your Honour. Could we have an IC number for this document, please. Excuse me. Could I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not until we get the number. Then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you have described to us the length of the border and the boundaries of the zone of defence. Can you tell us, in accordance with the principles, what should be the size of a zone or an area for a mechanised brigade like yours.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: For this size of brigade, under these conditions, the zone of defence, according to the front, should be 10 to 12 kilometres and about 15 kilometres in depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system Exhibit number 5D1284, please. Could we also have this exhibit in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can you see this document before you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me what this document represents.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: This is an order for defence received from the commander of the Pristina Corps in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we look at paragraph number 4, please, count number 4. Also in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, to avoid reading, we can see item 4 clearly before us. This is your order. Will you please tell us what the main task was.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: The main task was in the basic plan -- or rather, in the decision to organise defence, decisive defence in the assigned zone and to prevent a NATO aggression along this axis, as well as an incursion by Siptar terrorist forces in the zone of defence of the brigade, because the brigade was in the first belt of defence, so this territory had to be defended decisively.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Count 9, please. In B/C/S, it's the last page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, item 9, paragraph 2. That's what I'm interested in. It says here that you will implement in a planned and organised manner a coordinated action with the appropriate units of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says: "The Brigade Command shall implement in a planned and organised manner in its area of responsibility" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We see this on our screens. My question refers to the cooperation you had with the MUP organs, what sort of -- what was it like?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Well, it was quite correct and it was quite proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did the MUP forces ever re-subordinate you in the course of the war, or were they re-subordinated to your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, never were they re-subordinated to me or to my superior officer or to my unit. There were some attempts made in that -- to that effect. There were some orders coming from the commander of the Pristina Corps to re-subordinate parts of the MUP, but this was never actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With whom did you cooperate mostly in the MUP? What person?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: The only person I contacted with was the chief of the Urosevac SUP, Colonel Bogoljub Janicijevic. I only contacted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at the next sentence. The next sentence, same paragraph, continues: "Appropriate cooperation and coordinated action shall be implemented through the appropriate organs and authorities, government organs and local municipal organs." My question is: What was your cooperation with the civilian sector like?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Our cooperation was correct, just as it had been before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did the units of civil defence and civilian protection -- or rather, were they re-subordinated to you at any point in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: At no point were these units re-subordinated to my unit or to me. They belonged to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of combat activity together with these units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, we had no joint combat activities with these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did the army perhaps participate in the forming of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, there was no need, nor did we ever use that term, nor did we deal with that, because all the municipal assemblies were in power and they functioned throughout the war, albeit with difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the life of citizens was like and the economy, and so on. Was the judiciary functioning? Were the authorities functioning?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: All the judicial organs and the organs of government continued operating just as before, until the beginning of the aggression. True, they operated under difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was the civilian judicial system functioning?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, the judicial system, the MUP, everything was operating properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Because I would like to change the topic, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You wish to adjourn now? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, any more information on transcription?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I spoke with Mr. Reid. He indicates to me that to do a transcript of the entire Exhibit 950 completely in B/C/S would take five working days with the people we have available. And that's with tomorrow being the first working day. Now, he tells me to do it where we would insert B/C/S between the English that we currently have in Exhibit 950 would take twice as long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got me there, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- it got me too, Your Honour, but he explained to me that probably it is more difficult to do that because the -- during the translation, there are interruptions and speaking over each other; whereas, if the whole -- every word that is said on the tape is transcribed into Serbian, including the English that was spoken, that -- that only takes five days. But he told me it would take 10 or 11 days to do it as the ones we have for General Pavkovic and General Lukic, for example. So we would have two separate documents: One that's all in English; one that's all in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At this point in time, that does not make sense to me. I'll need to have that further investigated to see if I can understand what the difficulties are. I can't understand why the parts which are in B/C/S can't simply be typed out in a transcript in B/C/S, which is what's required.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that -- that was my initial reaction too, but it must be some ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll think about that and make an appropriate decision and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I would request, if you let me -- he tells me that some of this work is going to be done by the people in the field office in Zagreb and he's putting materials on the plane tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll know today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll adjourn now. Mr. Jelic, we have to interrupt your evidence. That's the end of today's proceedings. You'll have to return to continue your evidence tomorrow. That will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, overnight, until tomorrow, it's vital that you should have no discussion with anyone at all about any aspect of the evidence in this case. You can talk to people about whatever else you like, but you must not, with anyone, discuss the evidence. Now, would you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll see you tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday the 23rd day of November, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
